paragraphs.heading: Counting events in a stretch
paragraphs.text: The Poisson distribution tells you how likely each possible count of events is within a fixed stretch of time. It applies when the events arrive at a known average rate that stays the same, and when each one happens regardless of how long it has been since the one before. The count, written k, is a whole number that can be zero or larger. The stretch does not have to be time: the same idea works for counts in an area or in a volume.

paragraphs.heading: One number sets the shape
paragraphs.text: The whole distribution is controlled by one number, λ (lambda), the number of events you expect in the stretch. The chance of seeing exactly k events is (λᵏᵉ^(−λ))/k!. λ is the expected value of the count, and it is also its variance. If you are told a rate r instead, multiply it by the length of the stretch t to get λ = rt.

paragraphs.heading: When it fits
paragraphs.text: It suits settings where a great many events could happen but each one is rare. Two conditions matter. One event must not change the chance of another, and the average rate must not depend on what has already happened. When both hold, the count k follows a Poisson distribution.

paragraphs.heading: When it breaks down
paragraphs.text: Students arriving at a student union each minute probably do not fit. Their rate rises between classes and falls during them, and they tend to turn up in groups rather than one by one. Yearly counts of magnitude 5 earthquakes in a country may not fit either, if one big quake makes similar aftershocks more likely. A count that is guaranteed to be at least one is also not Poisson, though a zero-truncated version can model it.

paragraphs.heading: A call center example
paragraphs.text: Picture a call center that gets 3 calls a minute on average, at every hour of the day. If the numbers of calls in any two non-overlapping periods are independent, then the number of calls in any one minute is Poisson. The chance of getting between 1 and 4 calls in a minute is then about 0.77. The chance of getting none, or 5 or more, is about 0.23.

paragraphs.heading: Who found it
paragraphs.text: The distribution is named after the French mathematician Siméon Denis Poisson, who lived from 1781 to 1840. He published it in 1837 together with his theory of probability, in a work about wrongful convictions. Abraham de Moivre had given similar results back in 1711, which has led some authors to say the name should be his. Later, Simon Newcomb fitted it to the number of stars in a unit of space in 1860. In 1898 Ladislaus Bortkiewicz showed it described how often Prussian soldiers were killed by accidental horse kicks.
